title: Shameless nerve
core: All of these describe nerve — boldness that has crossed a line other people were respecting. The line differs: sometimes it's shame, sometimes rank, sometimes caution, sometimes the decent instinct to at least hide what you're doing. Most are the offended onlooker's verdict rather than a neutral description, so the choice usually encodes who is judging whom and on what grounds. One of them can be admiring, and one says the nerve isn't real at all.

words.nuance: The charge is **shamelessness itself** — the person should have been embarrassed and wasn't. It lives in a fixed frame (*had the effrontery to*), and what follows is always something the speaker finds indefensible. Rank is irrelevant here: an equal or a superior can show effrontery, because the offence is the missing blush, not the overstepped place.

The charge is **presumption of standing** — you acted above your station toward someone you owed deference to. It encodes a hierarchy that **effrontery** doesn't need: the private who questions the general has temerity; the general doing the same thing has none. It also carries a whiff of recklessness — nerve that hasn't reckoned with consequences.

The **only one here that can be a compliment**. It marks the ignored limit without ruling on it, so *an audacious plan* thrills and *an audacious lie* appalls, entirely on the sentence's say-so. Where the others arrive pre-loaded with disapproval, **audacious** waits to be told.

The scandal is **openness**, not the act. A brazen lie is told to your face by someone who knows you know — sneaking would concede that the rule mattered, and they won't. It's the only one with a verb (*brazen it out*: outlast an accusation by refusing to look ashamed), and it carries contempt for the audience, not just disregard.

The **only one where the nerve is fake**. It names a performance — swagger, loud talk, defiance staged for watchers — and using the word calls the bluff: the display is covering fear. The others describe boldness someone had; **bravado** describes boldness someone is advertising, hence *empty*, *false*, *a touch of*.

exam_note: The trap is reading all five as negatives: **audacious** is the fence-sitter that can praise, so in a positive-daring context it's the answer the other four can't be.
